description: Take the Brandenburg Gate apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of the gate: from Prussian peace monument to Napoleon's trophy, from war ruin to the symbol of reunified Germany.
intro: Berlin's most famous landmark is 26 meters of sandstone that has watched Prussian kings, Napoleon's army, Nazi rallies, and the fall of the Berlin Wall. This is how a city gate became the symbol of a reunited country.

sections.alt: The Quadriga on top of the Brandenburg Gate
sections.body: Commissioned by Frederick William II of Prussia and designed by Carl Gotthard Langhans, the gate was built between 1788 and 1791, modeled on the Propylaea of ancient Athens. Twelve Doric columns form five passageways through a structure 26 meters high and over 60 meters wide. It was first called the Friedenstor, the Peace Gate. In 1793 Johann Gottfried Schadow crowned it with the Quadriga: four horses pulling a chariot driven by the winged Victoria, goddess of victory, the first quadriga built since antiquity. The whole program carried one message, the absolutist's definition of peace: peace as the fruit of victorious arms.
sections.caption: The Quadriga, sculpted by Johann Gottfried Schadow and installed in 1793.
sections.credit: Yair Haklai, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: A gate for peace

sections.body: After Prussia's defeat at Jena-Auerstedt in 1806, Napoleon marched through the gate and carried the Quadriga off to Paris as a war trophy. When Napoleon fell, Prussian troops brought it home in 1814. For the occasion Karl Friedrich Schinkel reworked Victoria's standard: she received the Iron Cross crowned with the Prussian eagle, branding the victory as Prussia's.
sections.heading: Stolen, returned, rebranded

sections.alt: The Brandenburg Gate in ruins in May 1945 with a Soviet victory banner
sections.body: The Nazis adopted the gate as a party symbol and placed it on the axis of their planned world capital Germania. The war left it bullet-scarred; the Quadriga was destroyed, and only a single horse's head survived, now kept in the Märkisches Museum. When Soviet troops took Berlin in 1945, they raised the red banner of victory on the ruined Quadriga.
sections.caption: The gate in May 1945, with a Soviet victory banner on the ruined Quadriga.
sections.credit: Alexey Shapochkin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: Scarred by war

sections.alt: Crowds at the reopened border crossing at the Brandenburg Gate in December 1989
sections.body: When the Berlin Wall went up on 13 August 1961, it ran directly past the gate's western side. The gate stood in the death strip, unreachable from East and West alike, for 28 years. It was there, with the gate behind him, that Ronald Reagan demanded on 12 June 1987: Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!
sections.caption: The border crossing at the gate the day after it reopened, 23 December 1989.
sections.credit: Bundesarchiv, Bild 183-1989-1223-300 / CC-BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: Twenty-eight years behind the Wall

sections.body: On 9 November 1989 the Wall fell and thousands celebrated at the gate. On 22 December 1989 the crossing reopened, with Helmut Kohl walking through to meet Hans Modrow before a crowd of 100,000. The Quadriga was restored, the Iron Cross returned, and the gate itself was refurbished from 2000 to 2002. Today it is the symbol of reunified Germany: the finish line of the Berlin Marathon, the stage for New Year's Eve, and the first thing the world pictures when it thinks of Berlin.
sections.heading: The symbol of a reunited country
Rebuilt from a plaster cast
sections.body: The war left the gate pockmarked with bullets and shrapnel, and the Quadriga in ruins. A single horse's head survived, and it sits today in the Märkisches Museum. The Quadriga itself was saved by luck: a plaster cast made in 1942, three years before the destruction. In 1956, in a rare moment of East-West cooperation, sculptor Otto Schnitzer and the Hermann Noack foundry recreated the entire Quadriga from that cast. It was hoisted back on 14 December 1957, this time without the Iron Cross. After reunification the Quadriga came down again for renovation and the Iron Cross returned. From 2000 to 2002 the whole gate was restored for 6 million euros and reopened on 3 October 2002 with a new lighting concept. What you see today is a ruin that refused to stay one.

story_title: The story of the Brandenburg Gate
title: Brandenburg Gate

hotspots.title: The Quadriga
hotspots.text: Johann Gottfried Schadow's copper Quadriga has crowned the gate since 1793. Napoleon carried it to Paris as a war trophy in 1806; it came home in 1814. The original was destroyed in the Second World War; today's Quadriga is the 1957 recreation.

hotspots.title: Victoria's wings
hotspots.text: The wings are what make her Victoria. In classical iconography Nike alone among goddesses was winged, so the wings are victory's defining attribute. English accounts long said she began as Eirene, goddess of peace, but German research notes the 1789 building plans already called her Victoria.

hotspots.title: Victoria
hotspots.text: The winged charioteer is Victoria, goddess of victory. In 1814 Schinkel gave her a new standard: the Iron Cross crowned with the Prussian eagle, branding the victory over Napoleon as Prussia's.

hotspots.title: The Iron Cross
hotspots.text: Instituted on 10 March 1813, the Iron Cross was Prussia's first decoration open to every rank, from private to general. Schinkel set it in an oak wreath of 169 leaves and 90 acorns on Victoria's standard, turning the Quadriga into a monument to the victory over Napoleon.

hotspots.title: The Prussian eagle
hotspots.text: The crowned black eagle is the coat of arms of Prussia, one of Europe's oldest state emblems. Perched atop Victoria's standard, it brands the victory as specifically Prussian and ties the monument to the crown.

hotspots.title: The triumphal chariot
hotspots.text: A quadriga is a Roman triumphal chariot, the car in which victorious generals rode through Rome. Schadow's copper horses stand about 3.15 meters tall, modeled in just two poses with four different head positions. The form itself is the symbol: triumph.

hotspots.title: Mars sheathing his sword
hotspots.text: Mars, god of war, sits sheathing his sword: war laying down its arms, exactly the image a Peace Gate needs. The Academy of Arts chose Mars and Minerva over Schadow's own proposal of Diligence and Vigilance. Karl Wichmann carved him in sandstone; he was installed in July 1794.

hotspots.title: Minerva, guardian of the gate
hotspots.text: Minerva is the goddess of wisdom, and also the traditional protectress of city gates and doors: she literally guards this one. Schadow designed her; Johann David Meltzer carved her in sandstone in 1794. The original was destroyed in the war; today's figure is a 1951-52 replacement.

hotspots.title: The Triumph of Peace relief
hotspots.text: The attic relief shows Hercules driving away Discord while the goddess of peace arrives with an olive branch: just arms protecting innocence, as Langhans's 1791 brief demanded. A matching relief for the outer face was never made. The spot is still empty today.

timeline.text: Built to Carl Gotthard Langhans's design for Frederick William II of Prussia; first called the Peace Gate.
Johann Gottfried Schadow's Quadriga is installed on the attic.
After Jena-Auerstedt, Napoleon carries the Quadriga to Paris as a war trophy.
The Quadriga returns to Berlin; the goddess is rebranded as Victoria and given the Iron Cross.
The gate is bullet-scarred and the Quadriga destroyed; Soviet troops raise the red banner of victory.
Rare East-West restoration; the Quadriga is recreated from a 1942 plaster cast.
The Berlin Wall rises; the gate stands sealed in the death strip for 28 years.
Ronald Reagan at the gate: Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!
The Wall falls; thousands celebrate at the gate.
The border crossing reopens; Helmut Kohl walks through to meet Hans Modrow.
Official reunification ceremony at the gate; the flag is raised at midnight.
Full restoration; Pariser Platz becomes a pedestrian zone.
